proposal: Navarro argues that WTO most-favored-nation rules leave the United States with lower tariffs than most partners and recommends that Congress pass the United States Reciprocal Trade Act. It would let the President press partners to cut tariffs and nontariff barriers to U.S. levels and, if they refuse, raise U.S. tariffs to mirror theirs. He also suggests a destination-based border adjustment tax as a possible alternative.

status_summary: The administration pursued reciprocal tariffs by executive order rather than through the Act: Executive Order 14257 (2025-04-02) imposed a 10 percent baseline and higher country-specific rates under the emergency powers statute (IEEPA), and on 2026-02-20 the Supreme Court held 6 to 3 in Learning Resources v. Trump that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, after which Executive Order 14389 declared those duties no longer in effect the same day. A 10 percent temporary import surcharge under Section 122 ran from 2026-02-24 to 2026-07-24; USTR announced on 2026-07-23 Section 301 tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on 60 economies over forced-labor import bans, applying to entries from 2026-07-24 and published in the Federal Register on 2026-07-28, with some rates set net of the most-favored-nation duty and the lower tier tied partly to commitments in Agreements on Reciprocal Trade. On 2026-07-20 the President took Section 338 actions against Canada covering motor vehicles, alcoholic beverages and dairy, modified and widened with import bans on 2026-09-08; the motor-vehicle duties took effect on 2026-08-22 after a 3-day suspension, and a 2026-10-23 proclamation re-scoped them for entries from 2026-10-30, removing 22 tariff subheadings (mainly packaging and thin plywood) from the 50 percent duty and adding 100 (among them carpets, wood products and paints). Court of International Trade suits challenging the Section 301 tariffs were filed by importers (2026-07-24) and by 23 states joined by two governors (2026-08-03), and an order of 2026-08-13 placed them in a master case before a three-judge panel, with no ruling as of 2026-10-30 in the sources read. These are not country-by-country mirrors of partner tariffs, and no reciprocal trade legislation has been enacted, so the match to the Act's design is parallel.

timeline.event: Presidential memorandum directs Commerce and USTR to investigate non-reciprocal trade arrangements and propose reciprocal remedies for each trading partner.

Executive Order 14257 declares a national emergency over goods trade deficits and imposes a 10 percent additional duty on imports effective 2025-04-05, with higher country-specific rates from 2025-04-09, citing IEEPA.
Executive Order 14266 raises the additional tariff on Chinese goods to 125 percent and pauses higher country-specific rates for other partners for 90 days at a 10 percent baseline.
Supreme Court holds in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump (6 to 3) that IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs.
timeline.source: Supreme Court of the United States

timeline.event: Executive Order 14389 declares the IEEPA duties, including the reciprocal tariffs, no longer in effect and directs that collection stop as soon as practicable; a separate proclamation under Section 122 imposes a 10 percent import surcharge effective 2026-02-24 for 150 days (to 2026-07-24).

A three-judge panel of the Court of International Trade rules 2 to 1 that the 10 percent global tariffs imposed after the Supreme Court ruling, under Section 122, are invalid and unauthorized by law, as reported by the Associated Press; the report does not describe the scope of relief or any stay.

USTR announces Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies for failing to adopt and enforce forced-labor import bans: 10 percent for 17 listed economies (including Canada, Mexico, India and the UK), 10 or 12.5 percent net of the most-favored-nation rate for certain EU, Taiwan, Japan, Korea and Switzerland products, and 12.5 percent for others.
timeline.source: Office of the U.S. Trade Representative

timeline.event: Importers file suits at the Court of International Trade challenging the Section 301 forced-labor tariffs, including a proposed class action; the allegations are plaintiffs' claims, not findings.
USTR publishes the Section 301 forced-labor action notice (91 FR 47318); the duties apply to entries from 2026-07-24.

Twenty-three states, joined by the Office of the Governor of Kentucky and the Governor of Pennsylvania, file a complaint in the Court of International Trade (State of Oregon v. Trump, No. 26-03467, ECF 2) against the Section 301 forced-labor tariff action, alleging action in excess of statutory authority, arbitrary and capricious action and ultra vires action, and seeking a three-judge court, vacatur or a stay of the action, a declaration, injunctions and refunds; the allegations are the plaintiffs' claims, not findings.
timeline.source: U.S. Court of International Trade (complaint copy posted by doj.state.or.us)

timeline.event: A three-judge panel of the Court of International Trade issues Standard Procedural and Scheduling Order No. 26-01, creating the master case In Re Section 301 Forced Labor Cases (No. 26-cv-03555-3JP) for the Burlap and Barrel and Learning Resources importer suits and the State of Oregon suit, and providing for a representative sample case with consolidated briefing and a plaintiffs' steering committee; the order decides no claim.

A trade-press report states that the Court of International Trade will proceed first with a representative sample case in the Section 301 challenges, will set up a master case and a steering committee, and has scheduled oral argument in the sample case for 2026-09-30; the report does not give the order's date, and the later order selecting the sample case was not opened.

As recited in the 2026-10-23 proclamation, the Section 338 additional duties on certain products of Canada imposed by Proclamation 11048 of 2026-07-20 (effective 2026-08-19) and suspended for 3 days by Proclamation 11056 of 2026-08-18 take effect at 12:01 a.m. eastern time on 2026-08-22, after Canada, in the proclamation's words, reneged on its commitment on 2026-08-21.
USTR statement describes new Section 338 measures against Canada (duties and import bans on certain motor vehicles, dairy and alcohol), citing Canadian retaliation and discriminatory treatment.
timeline.source: Office of the U.S. Trade Representative

timeline.event: A presidential proclamation further modifies the scope of the Section 338 motor-vehicle duties on Canada: for goods entered on or after 12:01 a.m. eastern time on 2026-10-30, 22 HTSUS subheadings in Annex I Part A (including seaweed, polypropylene film, plastic packing, thin plywood, corrugated cartons, paper sacks and packaging and produce-sorting machinery) leave the 50 percent duty and 100 subheadings in Annex I Part B (including sweetened cocoa powder, paints, shampoos and soaps, MDF and fiberboard, wooden boxes and flooring, carpets under headings 5701 to 5705, window air conditioners, chest freezers, hand tools and archery equipment) are added, with HTSUS note 51(b)(3) amended by Annex II. Published on 2026-10-30 as Proclamation 11076 (91 FR 68861, FR Doc. 2026-22292); operative paragraph (1) states that the 50 percent duty applies in addition to Section 232 duties. It is an executive action under Section 338, not reciprocal tariff legislation.

uncertainties: The Court of International Trade ruling of 2026-05-07 on the Section 122 surcharge rests on an Associated Press report; as reported by a law firm, the injunction covered only three plaintiffs (the State of Washington, Burlap and Barrel, Inc. and Basic Fun, Inc.) and the Federal Circuit granted a temporary stay on 2026-05-12, and, as reported by a customs broker, it granted a stay pending appeal on 2026-06-11. The opinion and the stay orders were not read on a court site, so the stays are not shown as court events. Whether any Reciprocal Trade Act-type bill was introduced in the 119th Congress was not checked, because Congress.gov could not be opened in this review. How the Agreements on Reciprocal Trade interact with the post-ruling tariff structure, and the status of IEEPA refunds, were not verified from primary sources. The White House pages for the February 2025 review memorandum and the July 2025 de minimis order could not be read in this review. The Section 301 notice was read except for its closing portion and gave no expiry date for the duties. The states' complaint (ECF 2, filed 2026-08-03) was read on the Oregon attorney general's site and names 23 states plus the Office of the Governor of Kentucky and the Governor of Pennsylvania, where a news report counted 25 states; the order creating the master case (ECF 1, 2026-08-13) was read on the courtlistener storage host, with two pages of that copy unreadable. Later events reported in secondary accounts were not read in court records: a 2026-08-17 joint response, a 2026-09-03 protective order, the importers' complaint, a 2026-10-02 order for supplemental briefs due 2026-10-16, and the outcome of the 2026-09-30 hearing; a post on peopleofplay.com credited to a sample-case plaintiff reports an order of 2026-08-19 selecting the Learning Resources case as the sample case and staying the other two suits, which is not used as a source because it is a party-side account, and a trade-press report confirms only the sample-case procedure and the 2026-09-30 argument date. One secondary listing referred to a September 15 hearing, which the reports read do not support. No merits ruling or preliminary relief appears in any source read, and a full docket sheet was not read. The 2026-10-23 proclamation was published on 2026-10-30 as Proclamation 11076 (91 FR 68861, FR Doc. 2026-22292); operative paragraphs (1) to (8) were read in the GovInfo copy of that issue and re-read on govinfo.gov on 2026-10-30, including the 50 percent rate, the 12:01 a.m. eastern time 2026-10-30 effective time, the statement that the duties apply in addition to Section 232 duties, the CBP implementation authority and the delegation to USTR of the approval authority in 19 U.S.C. 1338(h); the annex tables appear only as images in that copy and were checked on the whitehouse.gov annex files. Proclamations 11048, 11056 and 11065 themselves were not opened (their dates and effects come from its recitals and the USTR statement). The full list of Canadian products still covered after the 2026-10-23 changes, and the trade effect of the duties, were not established.
